I wish I had your courage. I don't work for myself. I've often times thought about starting my own business, but jumping through all of the hoops seems prohibitively difficult. I wish you well with it.

Scary as you can imagine. Some months you feel like you're the smartest man in the world. No boss. Pride in what you do. Independence and pockets with cash in them. Other months you're looking at your bills wondering what you can push back a couple of weeks...because your pay 60 customers decided that means pay you in three or four months..maybe.

Insurance is a bitch. It wasn't bad last year, a little worse this year, and terrible the year after, but the Affordable Care Act is a killer for people starting a small business. Let's face it, health insurance is too expensive to afford on a monthly basis...and that means a tax penalty. Oh, speaking of taxes, you will be audited. The IRS loves the hell out of small companies. We don't hire as many lawyers to defend us. Instead they go after us, giving us a full rectal exam. Save every piece of paper. Cup of coffee on the way to work? Get a receipt. You never know with those bastards.

Scared? You should be. So whatever you start will never have the capital your competitors can get ahold of. If they ever wanted to undercut you out of the market, they'll do so...plus they have the connections to change regulations. Doesn't cost much to convince a state senator that solar panels need to be installed by someone on an approved list, you know?

So the game is rigged...it doesn't mean, however, that you shouldn't play. It's the only game in town. You just need to learn the table and budget accordingly.

Besides, the pay off is something you can't get anywhere else. Go for it!
Great summary. I would add in to do this part time until you can make it full time. I freelanced on the weekend, went to work during the week. Then when I had enough freelance to support me, I quit.
This is (one of the reasons) why the US economy is shit, in a nutshell. I own a small business in Hong Kong and there is almost none of the bullshit you speak of.
I do. It's awesome and less scary then waiting for someone else to dictate your future.

I remember the day I received my last check knowing that two weeks later I wouldn't get another one and I was all on my own to provide income. It's a scary step and you will have ups and downs. My best advice is for your wife to continue working a stable job until your business is secure enough to allow her to join

I have my own business. If you can figure out how to create value for some one you too can have one. The intenet lets us monetize anything! Just pick something you love to do. I will never (willingly) go back to clocking in.

Working for yourself you say? Well. Graphic design here. My experience is that my life is now pretty much nothing but work. I sleep much less, I work so much more. 40 hour week? HA! I'm often pushing 60+ hours a week. My life is scheduling around deadlines, trying to remember to file receipts, payments, debits, all that for tax season. I dream about work. Which, I have to say, is both very cool and very fucking annoying. There you are, enjoying your sleep, and then BAM you're dreaming about working, mentally going over what you need to accomplish. Then you wake yourself up, can't get back to sleep because you know sleep you was right and you really need more hours in the day.

So. Overall? It's great. I hate working with and for other people. I get to do something I absolutely love. Just be sure you're doing it for the right reasons. It's not easier. It's harder. But can be so worth it.

It is an emotional roller coaster. You go from the thrill of victory to the Oh Shit of taking care of customers often within minutes. It is exhilarating and exhausting. It is the most fun and the most terror. At the end of the day there is no better way to make a living.

Do your research. Figure out your costs and try to plan for the unforeseen issues like fluctuating gas prices and equipment breakdowns. And make sure you have some business in hand before you even launch. Cold calling or sitting around hoping for the phone to ring are the absolute worst part in my opinion. Being too busy is also a problem, but far better.

Godspeed.

/notsarcasticinthiscase

My favorite saying is "Plan your work, work your plan". So simple yet, as with most things, the devil is in the details (another favorite saying). You've put together a business plan (or so it seems) so now you need to work it. Being self employed is a great motivator but you have to be prepared to commit yourself to working 24/7, not that you work all the time but that you are at last always thinking about the many many things that are necessary. It's stuff like: how to grow the business, how to keep existing clients, how to save money, how to finance new equipment, etc etc. If this doesn't sound like you then I'd reconsider.

Grounds keeping is easy to get into because costs are relatively low and infrastructure minimal. What about your plan sets you apart from every other yahoo with some lawn tools and a truck? Not to mention the chains/franchises that have the appeal of brand recognition.

I recently started a small business with 2 friends and I can tell you, it's scary, but not as much as you'd think. The key is planning ahead for things that are ceirtan. You HAVE to keep in mind that you'll need to make yourself known in the market and this takes time and money. I can't say how long it will take, as it probably varies a lot depending on the area, the business, etc. but in my case it has been 4 months of almost no profit to build a good client portfolio.

Other important aspects include knowing how is the market rigged, as bobroland correctly pointed. Can your competitors undercut you in cost and quality of service? Can they bribe someone to enact special requirements? You get the idea.

Finally, once the work starts to pick up you'll probably get swamped, but it's quite a different sensation from being an employee. You don't feel exploited, on the contrary, you feel that your work actually makes a difference to someone. It's a great thing.

My advice in tl;dr form, plan as much as you can, get as much savings as you can and go for it.
